punctuated:
詩書所道哉？程頤曰：「聖王以求任輔相為先。」歐陽脩曰：「君之聖者以辨君子與小人。」盖政以人而舉，人既存，則政自無偏弊不舉之患，而治之在天下者可成也。
陛下欲求數君致治之績，獨可舍此而他務邪？亦惟有不敢易之心而已。天下之政，孰有出於人主之心者？况用人之際，又其本原所自之地哉！
聖制所謂「簡賢為輔，用君子不惑於小人」，誠灼見其必然而憂勤之心有不能自已者也。盖大君為天地之宗子，必有大臣以為宗子之家相。相之職，所以輔養君德而贊成政化，天子不可一日無者。豈惟夏商周為然？皐夔稷契之流，雖堯舜之世，亦不可無也。若其賢與否，則必辨之於先，而後可任之於後。苟辨之不明，用之不當，則天下之禍反有不可言者矣。何者？以匹夫之賤，而上與天子共事，其所為操縱予奪者，無一不為天下之所稟受。使心術或不正，而學識或不醇，則其所壞非如有司之一節一端而已。故必先有不敢易之心
translation_en:
…as described in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents? Cheng Yi said, “The sage kings gave priority to seeking out and appointing chief ministers.” Ouyang Xiu said, “A ruler’s sageliness consists in distinguishing gentlemen from petty men.” Government is carried out through people. Once the right people are in place, government naturally suffers neither from partiality and abuses nor from neglect, and good order throughout the realm can be achieved.
If Your Majesty wishes to attain the achievements in government of those several rulers, can you possibly abandon this and pursue other matters? All that is needed is a disposition that dares not take this lightly. What matter of government in the realm lies beyond the ruler’s mind? How much more is this true of employing men, where the very foundation of government originates!
Your Majesty’s decree speaks of “selecting worthy men as assistants, employing gentlemen, and not being misled by petty men.” This truly shows a clear recognition that things must be so, and a solicitous and diligent concern that cannot be restrained. The sovereign is the principal heir of Heaven and Earth, and must have great ministers to serve as the household stewards of that principal heir. The office of chief minister exists to nurture the ruler’s virtue and assist in bringing government and moral transformation to fruition; the Son of Heaven cannot do without it for a single day. Was this true only under the Xia, Shang, and Zhou? Men such as Gao, Kui, Ji, and Xie were indispensable even in the ages of Yao and Shun. Whether such men are worthy must first be discerned before they can subsequently be entrusted with office. If discernment is unclear and appointments inappropriate, the resulting calamities for the realm may instead be beyond description. Why is this? From the humble station of an ordinary man, a minister rises to work together with the Son of Heaven. In all that he controls or releases, grants or takes away, there is nothing whose effects the whole realm does not receive. If his intentions are in any way improper or his learning and understanding unsound, the damage he does is not confined to a single matter or aspect of administration, as with an official responsible for a particular charge. Thus one must first possess a disposition that dares not take this lightly…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
然後脩之身者無徃不實脩之身者既實則
出乎我者無乎不正而人之邪正自無所匿
於是擇其賢者而用之則輔相得矣臣於
今日豈以不得為憂哉特恐所以待之者不至
爾臣在草野間聞
朝廷用一大臣必極聳動以為諮謀親信將必
有出於恒品之外今上於
京師乃或有未然者臣願
陛下為之禮下務得其心而使盡其職凡遠猷大
畧不為羣議所詘一政一令必與之深言極
===
論而後布則小人雖欲肆其無所忌憚之私
以惑吾聽而其情已先覺矣盖小人之情不
過趨利避害去其所惡而求其所喜者而已
然亦必掩之而不甚露故利之來或遜且謝
之害之至或以為所分且蹈之夫辭之不力
則得之不固受之不力則去之不决及利害
至於必不可已則亟去與取之恐後也方其
有所勉而為之也其卒不可掩者已躍然於
甘言悅色之間即此試之小人之情可復遁
乎既得其情則宜亟去之去之不亟則或為

之害之至或以為所分且蹈之夫辭之不力

punctuated:
然後脩之身者無徃不實。脩之身者既實，則出乎我者無乎不正，而人之邪正自無所匿。於是擇其賢者而用之，則輔相得矣。臣於今日豈以不得為憂哉？特恐所以待之者不至爾。臣在草野間，聞朝廷用一大臣，必極聳動，以為諮謀親信，將必有出於恒品之外。今上於京師，乃或有未然者。臣願陛下為之禮下，務得其心，而使盡其職。凡遠猷大畧，不為羣議所詘；一政一令，必與之深言極論而後布，則小人雖欲肆其無所忌憚之私以惑吾聽，而其情已先覺矣。
盖小人之情，不過趨利避害，去其所惡而求其所喜者而已。然亦必掩之而不甚露，故利之來，或遜且謝之；害之至，或以為所分且蹈之。夫辭之不力，則得之不固；受之不力，則去之不决。及利害至於必不可已，則亟去與取之恐後也。方其有所勉而為之也，其卒不可掩者，已躍然於甘言悅色之間。即此試之，小人之情可復遁乎？既得其情，則宜亟去之。去之不亟，則或為
translation_en:
… Only then will self-cultivation be genuine in every respect. Once self-cultivation is genuine, everything that proceeds from oneself will be upright, and the depravity or uprightness of others will naturally have nowhere to hide. By then selecting and employing the worthy, one will obtain worthy chief ministers. How could your servant worry today that such men cannot be found? I fear only that the treatment accorded them may fall short. While living among the common people, whenever your servant heard that the court had appointed a great minister, I was deeply stirred, believing that the consultation and personal trust accorded him would surely exceed the ordinary. Now that I have come up to the capital, I find that this is sometimes not so. Your servant wishes Your Majesty to treat them with ritual courtesy and humility, strive to win their hearts, and enable them to discharge their duties fully. Let no far-reaching plan or grand strategy be thwarted by the multitude of opinions. Discuss every policy and every command with them deeply and exhaustively before promulgating it. Then, even if petty men wish to indulge their utterly unscrupulous private interests and confuse Your Majesty’s judgment, their true motives will already have been detected.
For the motives of petty men amount to no more than pursuing advantage and avoiding harm, shunning what they dislike and seeking what they enjoy. Yet they invariably conceal these motives rather than expose them too plainly. Thus, when advantage comes, they may defer to others and decline it; when harm approaches, they may regard it as their allotted portion and accept it. Unless they decline forcefully, they cannot securely obtain the advantage; unless they accept resolutely, they cannot decisively escape the harm. When advantage or harm reaches a point at which action can no longer be postponed, they hasten to escape the one and seize the other, fearing to fall behind. Even while they are forcing themselves to act this way, what ultimately cannot be concealed already shows plainly amid their sweet words and pleasing expressions. If they are tested by this, can the true motives of petty men still escape detection? Once their motives are known, they should be removed promptly. If they are not removed promptly, one may…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
他巧所中而猶未免於有惑隨有即覺隨覺
即去如是而已如是則君子小人不相尤君
子小人不相尤則動無所妨而天下之務自
無疑滯不舉之患矣臣請以
聖制所及數者言之禮樂不可以一日無此萬古
不易之論然其興也雖專重其實而亦未嘗
遂棄其文臣竊見近之所為禮者疎簡縱逸雖
所謂儀文之末亦未之有所為樂者殘缺廢
壞雖所謂聲容之細亦未之備盖不得其本
而安於苟且將就之習固如是也茍學校之
教有以維持而興起之則人心自無不正之
欲而其心自無不和之發凡見之宗廟朝廷
鄉黨之間自有以去其疎簡縱逸之習而補
其殘缺廢壞之弊將不俟於進退升降而節
不俟於鐘鼓管籥而和矣禮樂有不興者乎至夫教
化之所在其機係於人主之心而其應屬之
天下之廣萃英俊之士使之群遊於學讀書
窮理且或莫為之變而欲敺天下之愚民使
悉歸於禮讓和樂之域固已難矣莫若先以
恭儉忠厚躬行於上不為聲色土木貨利玩

他巧所中，而猶未免於有惑。隨有即覺，隨覺即去，如是而已。如是，則君子小人不相尤；君子小人不相尤，則動無所妨，而天下之務自無疑滯不舉之患矣。
臣請以聖制所及數者言之。禮樂不可以一日無，此萬古不易之論。然其興也，雖專重其實，而亦未嘗遂棄其文。臣竊見近之所為禮者，疎簡縱逸，雖所謂儀文之末，亦未之有；所為樂者，殘缺廢壞，雖所謂聲容之細，亦未之備。盖不得其本，而安於苟且將就之習，固如是也。茍學校之教有以維持而興起之，則人心自無不正之欲，而其心自無不和之發。凡見之宗廟、朝廷、鄉黨之間，自有以去其疎簡縱逸之習，而補其殘缺廢壞之弊。將不俟於進退升降而節，不俟於鐘鼓管籥而和矣。禮樂有不興者乎？
至夫教化之所在，其機係於人主之心，而其應屬之天下之廣。萃英俊之士，使之群遊於學，讀書窮理，且或莫為之變，而欲敺天下之愚民，使悉歸於禮讓和樂之域，固已難矣。莫若先以恭儉忠厚躬行於上，不為聲色、土木、貨利、玩
translation_en:
…be ensnared by his other cunning devices and still remain subject to confusion. As soon as such confusion arises, recognize it; as soon as it is recognized, remove him. That is all. In this way, gentlemen and petty men will not blame one another. If they do not blame one another, action will meet with no obstruction, and the affairs of the realm will naturally be free from the danger of being left undone through doubt and delay.
Your servant begs to discuss the several matters touched upon in Your Majesty’s decree. Rites and music cannot be dispensed with for even a single day: this is a judgment unchanging through all ages. Yet in reviving them, although primary weight is placed upon their substance, their outward forms have never therefore been discarded. Your servant humbly observes that what passes for ritual of late is perfunctory and lax. Even the lesser details of ceremonial forms are absent. What passes for music is incomplete and fallen into disrepair; even the minor details of sound and deportment have not been fully provided for. This is indeed what happens when people fail to grasp the fundamentals and settle comfortably into habits of expediency and making do. If instruction in the schools can sustain and revive them, people’s hearts will naturally harbor no improper desires, and nothing issuing from those hearts will lack harmony. In all that finds expression in the ancestral temples, at court, and within local communities, there will naturally be means to eliminate these perfunctory and lax habits and remedy these deficiencies and deterioration. There will then be due measure without waiting for the prescribed movements of advancing, withdrawing, ascending, and descending, and harmony without waiting for bells, drums, pipes, and flutes. How could rites and music fail to flourish?
As for moral transformation through instruction, its moving impulse lies in the ruler’s heart, while its response extends throughout the vast realm. Even when outstanding scholars are gathered together to study in the schools, read books, and investigate principle, some may remain unchanged. To seek, then, to lead the ignorant common people of the realm so that all enter a condition of ritual propriety, deference, harmony, and joy is certainly difficult. Nothing would be better than first personally practicing reverence, frugality, loyalty, and generosity at the highest level, without being swayed by sensual pleasures, building projects, material gain, or amusements…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
好之所移易而後徐以示於天下天下方以
前日之侈縱相安而一旦之所聞見乃如此
其心亦必悚然以思泠然以省茍一二大家
巨族頓悟而倡改之則人之樂從者衆矣選
課之法則臣於此有所深惜
祖宗之於士養之以道義而信之以賞罰其用也
不為之拘而其課之也幽明殿最各為之等
故人皆勉於其官而優於其事比者稍有兵
荒而納粟買官之人已滿吏部之簿矣雖有
才德滯於所用之期用未及而顛毛已號種
===
種能以壯節自勵者曽幾人哉又況黜陟之
施一惟流品是視茍不本於科甲之選高官
重秩未肯輕予則彼無所慕於中者又安有
所忌於外哉臣願嚴其僥倖覬覦之禁使冗
懦不職之徒一一謝去選惟其才而不盡拘
流品試之以官而課之以實如蘇洵所謂某
人廉吏也有某事以知其廉某人能吏也有
某事以知其能然後因其最否以加賞罰天
下之人望以其才自見者亦將知所變矣征

好之所移易，而後徐以示於天下。天下方以前日之侈縱相安，而一旦之所聞見乃如此，其心亦必悚然以思，泠然以省。茍一二大家巨族頓悟而倡改之，則人之樂從者衆矣。

translation_en:
…and not be swayed by such pleasures and indulgences, and only then gradually set this example before all under Heaven. People have grown accustomed to the extravagance and excess of former days; if what they suddenly hear and see is like this, they will surely be startled into reflection and brought to sober self-examination. If one or two great and powerful families abruptly awaken and take the lead in reform, many will gladly follow.
As for the methods of selection and performance evaluation, your servant finds here much cause for deep regret. In their treatment of scholars, the imperial ancestors nurtured them through moral principles and maintained their trust through rewards and punishments. They imposed no rigid restrictions on their employment, while in evaluating them they assigned distinct grades to the unworthy and worthy, the worst and best performers. Thus everyone exerted himself in office and became proficient in his duties. Recently, with only a little warfare and famine, the registers of the Ministry of Personnel have already filled with men who purchase office by contributing grain. Even those possessing ability and virtue must wait for appointment; before their turn comes, the hair on their heads is already sparse [?]. How many can still spur themselves on with vigorous resolve? Moreover, demotion and promotion depend solely on categories of recruitment. Unless a man entered through the civil-service examinations, high office and substantial rank are not readily granted him. If he thus has nothing to aspire to inwardly, what external restraint will he fear? Your servant wishes that prohibitions against seeking advancement through undeserved favor be strictly enforced, and that superfluous, weak, and incompetent officials all be dismissed. Select men solely for their abilities, without being wholly bound by their categories of recruitment; test them in office and evaluate them by their actual accomplishments. As Su Xun said: “So-and-so is an incorruptible official: a particular deed establishes his integrity. So-and-so is a capable official: a particular deed establishes his ability.” Then confer rewards and punishments according to the quality of their performance. Those throughout the realm who hope to distinguish themselves through their abilities will likewise understand how to change.
The trouble with taxation lies, for the most part, in excessive wasteful expenditure, which the officials responsible for fiscal accounting do nothing to reduce. It is not …

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
司會之不省勢不得也自京師言之食之仰
於江南歲數百萬而權勢所畜無藉之輩不
為國家分寸之益者乃至百千借其空名以
耗實費至有水旱饑饉之變則又加倍以取
於江南之民臣聞土曰窟則陷繼之江南之
民貧甚則江北可晏然以不顧乎况今邊境
之擾未甚妥帖前日榆林大同之役馬死食
匱所費不知幾千萬而無用之兵又坐食於
邊山陝之民丁運之法無不備舉老幼婦子
流離移析外患未除而內地已困寧不為可
懼邪臣欲去冗耗無用之費而革權門招集
之弊息江南之民以固根本邊境之擾但以
付之良將不用統制之屬帶挾僥倖之徒以
耗軍食而又復屯田之實省丁運之苦用固
無不足者也兵則先於生養安息之間為之
深計使不受役於私門而得給其俯仰奮迅
矯烈之氣又必常振勵之使之無所沮喪今
有一級之勞而大家右族訶譴奪去不敢仰
視將何所養以自奮乎况夫新舊逃流之兵
方以官法逼之復伍釜爨之用俱無可充又

司會之不省，勢不得也。自京師言之，食之仰於江南，歲數百萬，而權勢所畜無藉之輩，不為國家分寸之益者，乃至百千，借其空名以耗實費。至有水旱饑饉之變，則又加倍以取於江南之民。臣聞土曰窟，則陷繼之。江南之民貧甚，則江北可晏然以不顧乎？况今邊境之擾，未甚妥帖。前日榆林、大同之役，馬死食匱，所費不知幾千萬，而無用之兵又坐食於邊。山陝之民，丁運之法無不備舉，老幼婦子流離移析。外患未除，而內地已困，寧不為可懼邪？臣欲去冗耗無用之費，而革權門招集之弊，息江南之民，以固根本。邊境之擾，但以付之良將，不用統制之屬帶挾僥倖之徒以耗軍食，而又復屯田之實，省丁運之苦，用固無不足者也。

translation_en:
…that the officials responsible for fiscal accounts fail to economize; circumstances prevent them from doing so. Consider the capital: its food supply depends on Jiangnan, amounting to several million annually. Yet the disreputable men maintained by the powerful, who contribute not the slightest benefit to the state, number in the hundreds and thousands. They draw on actual resources under nominal appointments. When floods, droughts, or famine strike, twice as much is then exacted from the people of Jiangnan. Your servant has heard that when the earth becomes hollow, collapse follows [reading doubtful: 土曰窟]. If the people of Jiangnan become desperately poor, can those north of the Yangzi remain at ease and disregard them? Moreover, the present disturbances on the frontier have yet to be properly settled. In the recent campaigns at Yulin and Datong, horses died and provisions ran short; expenditure reached untold tens of millions. Meanwhile, useless troops sit idle on the frontier, consuming provisions. Among the people of Shanxi and Shaanxi, every means of conscripting men to transport supplies has been employed. Old and young, women and children wander displaced, their families scattered. Before the external threat has been eliminated, the interior is already exhausted. Is this not cause for fear? Your servant wishes to eliminate wasteful and useless expenditure and end the abuse whereby powerful households gather such retainers, giving the people of Jiangnan respite and thereby securing the foundation of the state. Frontier disturbances should simply be entrusted to capable generals, without employing commanders and their kind who bring along men seeking unearned advancement and consume military provisions. If, in addition, military agricultural colonies are restored to effective operation and the hardship of conscripted transport is reduced, resources will assuredly suffice.

As for the soldiers, careful provision must first be made for their livelihood, rest, and security, so that they are not compelled to serve private households and can support their parents and families. Their spirited courage and martial vigor must also be constantly encouraged, so that nothing dispirits them. As things stand, a soldier may earn merit by taking an enemy head, only for great households and powerful clans to berate him and strip him of it, until he dares not raise his eyes. What can then sustain his spirit and move him to exert himself? Moreover, soldiers who deserted and drifted away, whether recently or long ago, are now being forced by official law to rejoin their ranks, yet they lack even the means to furnish their cooking pots and hearths. Furthermore, …

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
其居無親戚往來之接其心之欲去已甚矣
衛所之官又以嚴刑深計鉤取其有彼方有
欲去之心而此又逐之使去遂矣而不去豈
人情哉欲兵之强而二者特不之詳臣所以
深慮也用刑之際洞照物情而不為所誑明
者皆足為之而法之輕重則有一定之制既
得其情必為之斷使貴賤無異施豪右寡弱
無異决則令之所出即無不從天下之奸當
必隨禁而革盖天下皆天子之民明勅於必
戮賞期於必得不待命而後知若是則豪右之
===
徒有所恃仗得以自脫而寡弱之人駢首就
死人之情孰不畏死而不求所以自脫哉此
尤
陛下之所宜置念者也夫數者之務酌之於古而
行之於今宜有不可易者而其弊猶若此
聖制所謂袪其弊而捄之欲化行政舉如
祖宗創業之初比隆前代者豈有他哉亦取諸人
而已孔子曰為政在人啓以下數君不過中
才之主一得其人且足以為治而况
陛下神聖天縱出於尋常萬萬者哉然臣於此竊

punctuated:
其居無親戚往來之接，其心之欲去已甚矣。衛所之官又以嚴刑深計鉤取其有，彼方有欲去之心，而此又逐之，使去遂矣，而不去豈人情哉？欲兵之强，而二者特不之詳，臣所以深慮也。
用刑之際，洞照物情而不為所誑，明者皆足為之。而法之輕重，則有一定之制。既得其情，必為之斷，使貴賤無異施，豪右寡弱無異决，則令之所出，即無不從，天下之奸當必隨禁而革。盖天下皆天子之民，明勅於必戮，賞期於必得，不待命而後知。若是，則豪右之徒有所恃仗，得以自脫，而寡弱之人駢首就死。人之情，孰不畏死而不求所以自脫哉？此尤陛下之所宜置念者也。
夫數者之務，酌之於古而行之於今，宜有不可易者，而其弊猶若此。聖制所謂袪其弊而捄之，欲化行政舉，如祖宗創業之初，比隆前代者，豈有他哉？亦取諸人而已。孔子曰：「為政在人。」啓以下數君，不過中才之主，一得其人，且足以為治，而况陛下神聖天縱，出於尋常萬萬者哉？然臣於此竊
translation_en:
…Where they live, they have no relatives with whom to exchange visits, and their desire to leave is already very strong. The officers of the guards and battalions further use harsh punishments and elaborate schemes to extract their possessions. Just when these men already wish to leave, the officers drive them away, bringing that wish to fruition. Would it accord with human nature for them to stay? To desire strong troops yet fail to examine these two matters closely—this is what deeply concerns your servant.
When administering punishments, discerning men are all capable of seeing clearly into the circumstances and avoiding deception. But the severity of penalties is governed by fixed rules. Once the facts have been established, judgment must be rendered. If punishments are applied alike to the eminent and the humble, and judgments are the same for the powerful and the defenseless, then every command issued will be obeyed, and wrongdoing throughout the realm will surely cease as prohibitions are enforced. All under Heaven are the Son of Heaven’s subjects. Make it clear that execution will certainly follow where prescribed, and that promised rewards will certainly be received, so that people understand without waiting for a command. If this is so, the powerful have support on which to rely and can secure their own release, while the defenseless go to their deaths side by side [?]. Who, by human nature, does not fear death and seek a means of escape? This especially deserves Your Majesty’s attention.
As for these several affairs, their principles, weighed against antiquity and put into practice today, ought to include things that cannot be changed; yet their abuses remain as described. Your Majesty’s decree speaks of removing these abuses and remedying them, wishing moral transformation to take effect and government to function as at the beginning of the ancestral emperors’ founding enterprise, matching the glory of earlier dynasties. What other means could there be? It is simply a matter of finding the right people. Confucius said, “The conduct of government depends on men.” The several rulers from Qi onward were merely men of middling ability; yet once they obtained the right men, they could govern well. How much more, then, can Your Majesty, whose sagely wisdom is Heaven-bestowed and surpasses the ordinary by countless degrees! Yet on this point your servant ventures…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
有說焉盖政雖舉於有人而身則所以取人
之本故孔子又曰取人以身欲得人而不先
脩乎身是其心之所存輕忽率易不能不累
於愛憎之私而用所不當用舍所不當舍者
有矣臣願
陛下急於脩身以端取人之則然所以脩身者又
非勉强矯拂之所能致必自君臣父子夫婦
昆弟之間以至於動靜語默一事一為之際
常加儆畏內省于中果當於理而不悖乎果
非其當然之則而狃於外誘乎使天理純明
===
私欲淨盡則身無有不脩而道無有不盡酬
酢斟酌自不謬於天下之是非苟用乎人其
用必當苟發於政其發必精治功之隆必能
追配
祖宗卓越古昔而有詩書之所不及載者矣彼漢
唐宋區區小補之治又惡足論哉然臣又聞
治不患於始之不得而難於終之有繼伏惟
陛下常存不敢易之心以守此不可易之道則
國家天下之幸非獨臣之幸也臣無任惓惓忠
愛之至臣謹對

punctuated: 有說焉。盖政雖舉於有人，而身則所以取人之本。故孔子又曰：「取人以身。」欲得人而不先脩乎身，是其心之所存輕忽率易，不能不累於愛憎之私，而用所不當用、舍所不當舍者有矣。臣願陛下急於脩身，以端取人之則。然所以脩身者，又非勉强矯拂之所能致，必自君臣父子夫婦昆弟之間，以至於動靜語默、一事一為之際，常加儆畏，內省于中：果當於理而不悖乎？果非其當然之則而狃於外誘乎？使天理純明，私欲淨盡，則身無有不脩，而道無有不盡。酬酢斟酌，自不謬於天下之是非。苟用乎人，其用必當；苟發於政，其發必精。治功之隆，必能追配祖宗，卓越古昔，而有詩書之所不及載者矣。彼漢唐宋區區小補之治，又惡足論哉？然臣又聞，治不患於始之不得，而難於終之有繼。伏惟陛下常存不敢易之心，以守此不可易之道，則國家天下之幸，非獨臣之幸也。臣無任惓惓忠愛之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…have something to say on this matter. Although government is carried out through having the right men, the ruler’s own person is the foundation for selecting them. Thus Confucius also said: “Select men on the basis of your own person.” If one wishes to obtain worthy men without first cultivating oneself, one’s disposition will be careless and heedless, inevitably encumbered by private likes and dislikes; one will then employ those who ought not to be employed and reject those who ought not to be rejected. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty make self-cultivation an urgent priority, thereby setting right the standard for selecting men. Yet self-cultivation cannot be attained through forced effort and constraint alone. In the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, and elder and younger brothers, and extending to activity and stillness, speech and silence, and every affair and action, one must constantly remain vigilant and reverent and examine oneself inwardly: “Does this truly accord with principle without violating it? Does this in fact depart from the proper standard through habituation to external temptations?” If heavenly principle is made wholly clear and selfish desires are utterly eliminated, one’s person will be fully cultivated and the Way fully realized. In responding to affairs and weighing decisions, one will naturally judge correctly what is right and wrong in the world. When employing men, one’s appointments will assuredly be fitting; when putting policies into effect, one’s measures will assuredly be sound. The greatness of these achievements in government will surely rival those of your imperial ancestors and surpass antiquity, reaching accomplishments beyond those recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. How, then, could the petty, piecemeal improvements in government under the Han, Tang, and Song merit discussion?

Yet your servant has also heard that the difficulty in governing lies less in achieving success at the outset than in sustaining it to the end. I humbly hope that Your Majesty will always maintain a disposition that dares not take things lightly, thereby preserving this unalterable Way. This would be a blessing for the state and all under Heaven, and not merely for your servant. Your servant cannot contain his utmost earnest loyalty and devotion. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
矣
嗣大歷服十又五年
萬幾有一日二日之勤羣臣有三德六德之俊
固已度越古今增光
祖宗矣顧乃不鄙韋布進之于
廷詢以古人致治之由一時救弊之術臣有以
仰窺
聖心之萬一矣且臣天下之民也
陛下所欲聞天下之事也與天下之民計天下之
事此所謂舍己而從人樂善而忘勢者臣雖
===
至愚安敢不盡况黎獻帝臣之願方齒于萬
國之舉布衣當世之心或兾於一言之獻哉
陛下之所問者人與法也臣之所欲言者本與幾
也臣甞思之天生一世之人自足以周一世
之事天眷一代之君亦必付以一代之賢事
待人而後行人得君而後用是盖有幾與本
存乎其間故唐虞無自致之運而當時有可
致之人禹益非易擇之人而當時有能擇之
主此幾說也亦本之說也舍是而論治非臣
之愚所能臆度也請稽古證之前代繼統之

punctuated:
矣。嗣大歷服十又五年，萬幾有一日二日之勤，羣臣有三德六德之俊，固已度越古今，增光祖宗矣。顧乃不鄙韋布，進之于廷，詢以古人致治之由、一時救弊之術，臣有以仰窺聖心之萬一矣。且臣天下之民也，陛下所欲聞天下之事也。與天下之民計天下之事，此所謂舍己而從人、樂善而忘勢者。臣雖至愚，安敢不盡？况黎獻帝臣之願，方齒于萬國之舉；布衣當世之心，或兾於一言之獻哉！
陛下之所問者人與法也，臣之所欲言者本與幾也。臣甞思之：天生一世之人，自足以周一世之事；天眷一代之君，亦必付以一代之賢。事待人而後行，人得君而後用，是盖有幾與本存乎其間。故唐虞無自致之運，而當時有可致之人；禹益非易擇之人，而當時有能擇之主。此幾說也，亦本之說也。舍是而論治，非臣之愚所能臆度也。請稽古證之：前代繼統之
translation_en:
…Indeed. For fifteen years since succeeding to the great imperial charge, Your Majesty has diligently attended, day after day, to the myriad affairs of government; among your ministers are outstanding men possessing the three virtues or the six virtues. You have assuredly surpassed past and present and added glory to your ancestors. Yet you have not disdained men in plain cloth, but have brought them before the court and questioned them about how the ancients achieved good government and how the abuses of the present might be remedied. Through this, your servant has been able to glimpse a fraction of your sagely intentions. Moreover, your servant is one of the people of the realm, and what Your Majesty wishes to hear concerns the affairs of the realm. To consult the people of the realm about its affairs is what is meant by setting aside one’s own views to follow others, and delighting in goodness while forgetting one’s exalted position. Though your servant is exceedingly foolish, how could I dare not express myself fully? All the more so now that, aspiring to be among the worthy men who serve the emperor, I have just been included among those recommended from throughout the realm; might not a commoner’s desire to serve his age find fulfillment in the offering of a single word?
What Your Majesty asks about concerns men and institutions; what your servant wishes to discuss concerns foundations and incipient opportunities. Your servant has reflected upon this: the people Heaven brings forth in any age are themselves sufficient to attend to that age’s affairs; when Heaven favors the ruler of a dynasty, it must also entrust him with that dynasty’s worthy men. Affairs await the right men before they can be carried out, and men must find a ruler before their abilities can be employed. Incipient opportunities and foundations surely lie within this relationship. Thus, in the ages of Tang and Yu, there was no course of fortune that brought about good government by itself, but there were men capable of bringing it about. Yu and Yi were not men easily selected, but there were rulers capable of selecting them. This illustrates incipient opportunities, and it also illustrates foundations. To discuss government apart from these is beyond what your foolish servant can conjecture. Allow me to examine antiquity to substantiate this: among the rulers of former dynasties who succeeded to the imperial line…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
君賢而可稱者若夏之啓商之中宗高宗周
之成康是已若禹道之承有扈之伐夏啓之
治也自度於天命祗懼於治民中宗之治也
習養於舊勞建事於學古高宗之治也無敢
昏逾嗣文武之大訓成王所以追配於前人
奉答光命保弘濟之艱難康王所以端命於
上帝夫其致如是之治亦誠足以為一代之
君矣求其當時任事之臣則有非後世之所
能及者且官已倍於惟百事必位於惟能而
輔相之臣又皆極一時之選其在夏啓則有
===
若伯益之施澤其在中宗則有若巫咸之乂
王伊陟臣扈之格帝其在高宗則有若甘盤
之舊學傅說祖己之直言成王之時則周公
為之師召公為之保也康王之世則召公之
敬保畢公之率下也宿德元老授天下之大
柄豐功偉烈揚不世之洪休唐虞以降不可
及已雖然輔相不容以易得責任每病其不
專是以啓立而益為佐命之首中宗起而巫
咸受每事之咨高宗諒陰而傅說有代言之
托成王襁褓周公負扆以朝諸侯康王皮冕

punctuated:
君賢而可稱者，若夏之啓、商之中宗、高宗、周之成康是已。若禹道之承、有扈之伐，夏啓之治也；自度於天命，祗懼於治民，中宗之治也；習養於舊勞，建事於學古，高宗之治也。無敢昏逾，嗣文武之大訓，成王所以追配於前人；奉答光命，保弘濟之艱難，康王所以端命於上帝。夫其致如是之治，亦誠足以為一代之君矣。求其當時任事之臣，則有非後世之所能及者。且官已倍於惟百，事必位於惟能，而輔相之臣又皆極一時之選。其在夏啓，則有若伯益之施澤；其在中宗，則有若巫咸之乂王，伊陟、臣扈之格帝；其在高宗，則有若甘盤之舊學，傅說、祖己之直言；成王之時，則周公為之師，召公為之保也；康王之世，則召公之敬保，畢公之率下也。宿德元老，授天下之大柄；豐功偉烈，揚不世之洪休。唐虞以降，不可及已。

雖然，輔相不容以易得，責任每病其不專。是以啓立，而益為佐命之首；中宗起，而巫咸受每事之咨；高宗諒陰，而傅說有代言之托；成王襁褓，周公負扆以朝諸侯；康王皮冕
translation_en:
…among the rulers who inherited the throne in earlier dynasties, those worthy of praise for their virtue include Qi of Xia, Zhongzong and Gaozong of Shang, and Cheng and Kang of Zhou. Continuing Yu’s Way and campaigning against Youhu characterized the government of Qi of Xia. Measuring himself against Heaven’s Mandate and governing the people with reverent apprehension characterized Zhongzong’s government. Being nurtured through earlier hardships and establishing affairs through the study of antiquity characterized Gaozong’s government. Daring neither to be heedless nor to transgress, and continuing the great teachings of Kings Wen and Wu, King Cheng thereby matched the achievements of his predecessors. Reverently responding to the glorious mandate and preserving what had been brought to completion through great difficulty, King Kang thereby secured his mandate from the Lord on High. In achieving government such as this, they were indeed worthy to be rulers of their age. If we examine the ministers then entrusted with affairs, we find men whom later generations could not equal. Moreover, official posts had already doubled from the original hundred, and appointments to conduct affairs were necessarily reserved for the capable; the assisting chief ministers were also the finest men of their time.

Under Qi of Xia, there was Bo Yi, who spread beneficence. Under Zhongzong, there was Wu Xian, who assisted the king in governing, and Yi Zhi and Chen Hu, who rectified their sovereign. Under Gaozong, there was Gan Pan, his former teacher, and Fu Yue and Zu Ji, who spoke forthrightly. In King Cheng’s time, the Duke of Zhou served as his Preceptor and the Duke of Shao as his Guardian. In King Kang’s reign, the Duke of Shao guarded him reverently, while the Duke of Bi led the subordinate officials. Venerable elders of long-established virtue were entrusted with the great authority of the realm; through magnificent achievements and mighty deeds, they displayed blessings rarely seen in any age. Since the days of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, none could equal them.

Nevertheless, assisting chief ministers cannot be considered easy to find, and the assignment of responsibility is often flawed by its failure to vest authority fully in them. Thus, when Qi ascended the throne, Yi became foremost among those assisting him in fulfilling his mandate. When Zhongzong arose, Wu Xian was consulted on every matter. When Gaozong observed mourning in silence, Fu Yue was entrusted with speaking on his behalf. While King Cheng was still in swaddling clothes, the Duke of Zhou stood with his back to the royal screen to receive the feudal lords in audience. King Kang, wearing the leather ceremonial cap…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
召公秉周以定嗣續然明良固難於會合而
邪正亦易於混淆苟求之不切則樂道者不
能改畎畝之心擇之不精則治水者或至於
汩陳之患宋程頤曰聖君以求任輔相為先
而歐陽脩亦有辨君子小人情狀之說人君
立天下之本以操天下之幾亦期於如此而
已然輔相之職必得君子居之而後可以進
天下之君子必不使小人間之而後可以退
天下之小人不然則邪正之辨不明賢否之
迹終混而天下之勢卒墮於不可支持其本
===
既失其幾亦亡以至於此可不為太息耶是
則任相之重可知也而其本則在於君身
陛下天縱聰明不待勉强
聖德純固無假脩為脩身之道固已無待於愚臣
之言矣輔相之臣取自
簡在固無待於所謂擇臣亦無所容其說也然
而
清問所及乃若不足焉蓋勅命之歌交賡於無
虞之時如傷之視加意於丕冒之國至治之
君大抵然也竊惟天下之大本視操舍為存

召公秉周以定嗣續。然明良固難於會合，而邪正亦易於混淆。苟求之不切，則樂道者不能改畎畝之心；擇之不精，則治水者或至於汩陳之患。宋程頤曰：「聖君以求任輔相為先。」而歐陽脩亦有辨君子小人情狀之說。人君立天下之本，以操天下之幾，亦期於如此而已。然輔相之職，必得君子居之，而後可以進天下之君子；必不使小人間之，而後可以退天下之小人。不然，則邪正之辨不明，賢否之迹終混，而天下之勢卒墮於不可支持。其本既失，其幾亦亡，以至於此，可不為太息耶？是則任相之重可知也，而其本則在於君身。
陛下天縱聰明，不待勉强；聖德純固，無假脩為。脩身之道，固已無待於愚臣之言矣。輔相之臣，取自簡在，固無待於所謂擇臣，亦無所容其說也。然而清問所及，乃若不足焉。蓋勅命之歌，交賡於無虞之時；如傷之視，加意於丕冒之國。至治之君，大抵然也。竊惟天下之大本，視操舍為存
translation_en:
…the Duke of Shao took charge of Zhou [?] to secure the succession. Yet an enlightened sovereign and worthy ministers are indeed difficult to bring together, while the wicked and the upright are easily confused. If the search is insufficiently earnest, those who delight in the Way cannot be moved from their resolve to remain among the fields; if selection is insufficiently discerning, those charged with controlling the waters may instead bring about the calamity of disrupting the established order. Cheng Yi of the Song said, “A sage ruler gives priority to seeking and appointing chief ministers.” Ouyang Xiu likewise discussed distinguishing the dispositions and conduct of gentlemen from those of petty men. In establishing the foundation of All-under-Heaven and grasping the crucial springs of its affairs, a ruler seeks nothing beyond this. Yet only when gentlemen occupy the offices of chief minister can the gentlemen of All-under-Heaven be advanced; only when petty men are prevented from intruding can the petty men of All-under-Heaven be dismissed. Otherwise, the distinction between wickedness and uprightness will remain unclear, the conduct of the worthy and unworthy will ultimately be confused, and the affairs of All-under-Heaven will finally fall into a condition that cannot be sustained. Once the foundation is lost, control of the crucial springs of affairs is lost as well. When matters reach this point, can one refrain from a deep sigh? From this we may understand the gravity of appointing chief ministers; its foundation, however, lies in the ruler himself.
Your Majesty is endowed by Heaven with intelligence and discernment, without needing strenuous effort; your sagely virtue is pure and firm, without requiring cultivation. As regards self-cultivation, you surely have no need of the words of your foolish servant. Your chief ministers have been chosen through your own discerning consideration; you surely have no need of what is called the selection of ministers, and there is no room for further argument on that subject. Nevertheless, the matters addressed in your august inquiry suggest that you still regard your accomplishments as insufficient. Indeed, songs of admonition and command were exchanged in peaceful times, and care for the people, treating them as though they were injured, received particular attention even in a realm already broadly sheltered by royal virtue. Rulers who achieve the highest order generally act thus. I humbly reflect that the great foundation of All-under-Heaven, depending on whether it is held fast or let go, is preserved…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
亡天下之大幾以得失為治亂況立天下之
事易成天下之事難用天下之人易擇天下
之人難謂天下之事易成也以文王之德必
百年而後洽謂天下之人易擇也以帝堯之
聖且四凶之未除文王帝堯猶至於此則非
文王與帝堯者可不知所謹耶且世道有升
降之宜治道有倚伏之勢凡其始也與治同
道故擇人精而立法亦精其久也以漸而弛
故擇人懈而守法亦懈然天下之事不患其
廢弛恃吾有以振之天下之人不患其混淆
===
恃吾有以擇之爾
今日之事法久弊生天下之大萬事之繁固未
易舉而急務所在則若禮樂若教化若選才
課績若征賦兵刑凡
聖制之所及者是矣和序未協於幽明禮樂未和
於上下科目求人而或有遺才之嘆銓曹授
任而或有失職之譏征賦方悉而縣官告乏
兵刑一舉而百姓稱煩夫法者
祖宗共天下而立者也斟酌于古今之宜權度于
時俗之變

punctuated:
亡；天下之大幾，以得失為治亂。況立天下之事易，成天下之事難；用天下之人易，擇天下之人難。謂天下之事易成也，以文王之德，必百年而後洽；謂天下之人易擇也，以帝堯之聖，且四凶之未除。文王、帝堯猶至於此，則非文王與帝堯者，可不知所謹耶？且世道有升降之宜，治道有倚伏之勢。凡其始也，與治同道，故擇人精而立法亦精；其久也，以漸而弛，故擇人懈而守法亦懈。然天下之事，不患其廢弛，恃吾有以振之；天下之人，不患其混淆，恃吾有以擇之爾。
今日之事，法久弊生，天下之大，萬事之繁，固未易舉。而急務所在，則若禮樂，若教化，若選才課績，若征賦兵刑，凡聖制之所及者是矣。和序未協於幽明，禮樂未和於上下；科目求人，而或有遺才之嘆；銓曹授任，而或有失職之譏；征賦方悉，而縣官告乏；兵刑一舉，而百姓稱煩。夫法者，祖宗共天下而立者也，斟酌于古今之宜，權度于時俗之變。
translation_en:
…or perishes; at the great turning points of the realm, success or failure determines order or disorder. Moreover, it is easy to initiate the affairs of the realm but difficult to bring them to completion; easy to employ the people of the realm but difficult to select them. If one says that the affairs of the realm are easily brought to completion, even with King Wen’s virtue, a hundred years were needed before his influence fully spread. If one says that the people of the realm are easily selected, even with Emperor Yao’s sagacity, the Four Evildoers had yet to be removed. If even King Wen and Emperor Yao encountered such difficulties, can those who are neither King Wen nor Emperor Yao fail to recognize the need for caution? Furthermore, the course of the world has its conditions of rise and decline, and governance has its tendencies toward reversals of fortune. At the beginning, everything follows the path of good order: thus men are selected with care, and laws are likewise established with care. Over time, things gradually become lax: thus the selection of men grows careless, and observance of the laws likewise grows careless. Yet in the affairs of the realm, we need not fear neglect and decay, provided we have the means to revive them; among the people of the realm, we need not fear the intermingling of worthy and unworthy, provided we have the means to distinguish and select them.
In present affairs, laws long in force have given rise to abuses. Given the vastness of the realm and the multiplicity of its affairs, these certainly cannot easily be enumerated. The urgent tasks, however, concern rites and music, moral instruction, the selection of talent and assessment of performance, taxation, military affairs, and punishments—all those matters touched upon in Your Majesty’s decree. Harmony and proper order have not been achieved between the unseen and visible realms; rites and music have not brought harmony between those above and those below. Men are sought through the examinations, yet there are sometimes lamentations that talent has been overlooked. The personnel authorities assign offices, yet there are sometimes criticisms that men are unsuited to their duties. Taxes are collected in full, yet the government reports shortages. Whenever military or penal measures are undertaken, the common people complain of burdensome interference. Now, the laws are what Your Majesty’s ancestors established together with the realm, weighing what was appropriate in ancient and modern times and taking account of changes in contemporary customs…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
貽謀燕翼至于今日太平之盛百有餘年豈惟
百年萬世守之萬世之盛也而使其弊至于
此則奉行者何所辭其責哉夫天下之所以
治者有紀綱而已矣綱舉而目張紀約而條
貫輔相固天下之紀綱也會萃束縛之間有
轉動丰采之異舒徐談笑之頃有磐石泰山
之安相重於朝廷法行於天下澤被於生民
固也故端本以擇相用相以操幾范祖禹有
言天子之職在擇一相一相擇十使蘇軾告
其君亦以為任時不如任法任法不如任人
===
相得其人則諸司百執事皆得其人而天下
之治成矣且天下之治未有出於禮樂者禮
序而樂和天下之大治也使君聖於上相賢
於下相得而甚驩和序之大節也由是而有
教化則四方風動而禮樂行也由是而選才
則多士克生而教化洽也由是而課績則百
工惟時而才能效也用是才以任征賦則簿
計克實者不至於妨民撫字心勞者不傷於
奉公也用是才以御兵刑則六師之張皇可
以為邦之翰五刑之明允可以全民之衷也

punctuated:
貽謀燕翼，至于今日太平之盛，百有餘年。豈惟百年？萬世守之，萬世之盛也。而使其弊至于此，則奉行者何所辭其責哉？夫天下之所以治者，有紀綱而已矣。綱舉而目張，紀約而條貫。輔相固天下之紀綱也。會萃束縛之間，有轉動丰采之異；舒徐談笑之頃，有磐石泰山之安。相重於朝廷，法行於天下，澤被於生民，固也。故端本以擇相，用相以操幾。范祖禹有言：「天子之職在擇一相，一相擇十使。」蘇軾告其君，亦以為任時不如任法，任法不如任人。相得其人，則諸司百執事皆得其人，而天下之治成矣。
且天下之治，未有出於禮樂者。禮序而樂和，天下之大治也。使君聖於上，相賢於下，相得而甚驩，和序之大節也。由是而有教化，則四方風動而禮樂行也；由是而選才，則多士克生而教化洽也；由是而課績，則百工惟時而才能效也。用是才以任征賦，則簿計克實者不至於妨民，撫字心勞者不傷於奉公也。用是才以御兵刑，則六師之張皇可以為邦之翰，五刑之明允可以全民之衷也。
translation_en:
…They left plans for their descendants’ security, bringing about the flourishing peace of today, more than a hundred years later. Why should it last only a hundred years? If maintained for ten thousand generations, its flourishing would endure for ten thousand generations. Yet abuses have been allowed to reach this point: how can those charged with implementing these laws evade responsibility? What brings order to the realm is simply its guiding framework. When the main cord is raised, the meshes of the net spread open; when the governing principles are concise, the particulars fall into order. Chief councilors are indeed the guiding framework of the realm. Amid gathering and binding things together, they possess an extraordinary capacity to set affairs in motion and lend them distinction [?]; even while speaking and laughing at ease, they provide the stability of a massive rock or Mount Tai. When chief councilors carry weight at court, laws operate throughout the realm and benefits extend to the people: this is the natural result. Thus one rectifies the foundation by choosing chief councilors and employs them to direct the crucial workings of government. Fan Zuyu said, “The Son of Heaven’s duty lies in choosing one chief councilor; that chief councilor chooses ten commissioners.” Su Shi likewise told his sovereign that relying on circumstances was inferior to relying on laws, and relying on laws was inferior to relying on people. If the right person becomes chief councilor, all the offices and their officials will likewise be staffed by the right people, and good government throughout the realm will be achieved.
Moreover, good government in the realm has never gone beyond rites and music. Rites establish order and music creates harmony: this is the realm’s great good governance. When the ruler above is sagely and the chief councilor below is worthy, and they find deep satisfaction in working together, this is the cardinal principle of harmony and order. If moral instruction proceeds from this, all regions will respond as grass bends before the wind, and rites and music will prevail. If the selection of talent proceeds from this, many worthy men will arise, and moral instruction will spread everywhere. If the assessment of achievements proceeds from this, all officials will perform their duties at the proper time, and talent will prove effective. Employ such talent to administer taxation, and those who keep accurate accounts will not thereby burden the people, while those who labor devotedly to nurture them will not thereby compromise their public duties. Employ such talent to direct military affairs and punishments, and the Six Armies, arrayed in their might, can serve as the state’s bulwark, while the Five Punishments, applied with discernment and fairness, can preserve the people’s innate moral nature.

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
故君相和而禮樂興禮樂興而教化作教化
作而才能著才能著而庶績熈是相也者佐
其君以操天下之幾救天下之弊以成天下
之治者擇之誠不可不精而任之誠不可不
專也臣願
陛下格致以窮理使天下之事無不知存省以居
敬使外物之誘不能奪視聽言動一遵乎禮
好惡用舍不違乎天則為治之道備具於一
身而取人之則足示乎天下今之大臣固
陛下之所簡知者也然相知雖深而相信或不足
===
則展布之體不足以償畏避之私核實之情
且有以貽疑間之迹臣雖至愚亦知其不可
也臣願
陛下勿為形迹之可疑必使意氣之相得如文王
之罔知如成王之勿誤嘉謨入告有聽受而
無難宣力四方惟所施而不問禮樂教化惟
期於成天下之俗選才課績惟期於得天下
之賢征賦兵刑惟期於畢天下之務
穆清之上高拱無為覆載之間旁達無間若是
而法有未行治有未成者臣未之信也

punctuated:
故君相和而禮樂興，禮樂興而教化作，教化作而才能著，才能著而庶績熈。是相也者，佐其君以操天下之幾，救天下之弊，以成天下之治者。擇之誠不可不精，而任之誠不可不專也。
臣願陛下格致以窮理，使天下之事無不知；存省以居敬，使外物之誘不能奪。視聽言動，一遵乎禮；好惡用舍，不違乎天。則為治之道備具於一身，而取人之則足示乎天下。今之大臣，固陛下之所簡知者也。然相知雖深，而相信或不足，則展布之體不足以償畏避之私，核實之情且有以貽疑間之迹。臣雖至愚，亦知其不可也。
臣願陛下勿為形迹之可疑，必使意氣之相得。如文王之罔知，如成王之勿誤。嘉謨入告，有聽受而無難；宣力四方，惟所施而不問。禮樂教化，惟期於成天下之俗；選才課績，惟期於得天下之賢；征賦兵刑，惟期於畢天下之務。穆清之上，高拱無為；覆載之間，旁達無間。若是而法有未行、治有未成者，臣未之信也。
translation_en:
Thus, when ruler and chief ministers are in harmony, rites and music flourish; when rites and music flourish, moral instruction arises; when moral instruction arises, talent and ability become manifest; and when talent and ability become manifest, all undertakings prosper. Chief ministers assist their ruler in grasping the pivotal workings of the realm, remedying its defects, and bringing it to good order. They must indeed be selected with the utmost care and entrusted wholeheartedly with their responsibilities.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would investigate things and extend knowledge to fathom principle, leaving nothing in the affairs of the realm unknown; and preserve and examine your mind to abide in reverence, so that the enticements of external things cannot sway you. In looking, listening, speaking, and acting, follow ritual propriety throughout; in liking and disliking, employing and dismissing, do not depart from Heaven. Then the Way of governing will be fully embodied in your own person, and your standards for selecting men will suffice as an example to the realm. The present great ministers are certainly men whom Your Majesty has selected and knows well. Yet even where mutual understanding is profound, mutual trust may be insufficient. In that case, the arrangements for exercising their abilities will not suffice to counterbalance their private fears and evasions, and an intention to ascertain the facts may leave signs of suspicion and estrangement. Though your servant is exceedingly ignorant, even I know that this will not do.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would avoid outward conduct liable to arouse suspicion and ensure a mutual accord of spirit and purpose: like King Wen’s “not knowing,” and King Cheng’s “not mistaking.” When excellent plans are presented, hear and accept them without making difficulties; when ministers exert themselves throughout the land, allow them to carry out their work without questioning them. In rites, music, and moral instruction, seek only to perfect the customs of the realm; in selecting talent and assessing performance, seek only to obtain the realm’s worthy men; in levies, taxation, military affairs, and punishments, seek only to accomplish the realm’s business. Above, in the serene purity of the imperial court, you may sit with hands folded, governing without intervention; throughout all that Heaven covers and Earth bears, your influence will reach everywhere without obstruction. With matters thus arranged, your servant cannot believe that any law would remain unimplemented or good government remain unachieved.

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
聖制之所及者臣既畧露其悃愊矣然惓惓之心
竊有不能自已者焉夫治功難保人情易盈
是以行恒畏於不矜聖或暫於罔念虞舜之
聖伯益且戒其無荒成王之賢周公必戒其
無逸今
陛下之德將以為舜也將以卓越成王也臣敢不
致其愛耶惟願
陛下益加懋德正其本而不移益廣求賢操其幾
而不失防微杜漸常若我
祖宗創業之初持盈守成遠追古帝王致治之盛
===
久大之業自是而可以無疆熈皥之休自是
而可以不替此則愚臣區區之誠而亦
陛下所欲聞之實也
陛下倘不以臣言為不可用豈特愚臣之幸哉臣
干冒
天威不勝隕越之至臣謹對

而可以不替此則愚臣區區之誠而亦

punctuated: 聖制之所及者，臣既畧露其悃愊矣。然惓惓之心，竊有不能自已者焉。夫治功難保，人情易盈，是以行恒畏於不矜，聖或暫於罔念。虞舜之聖，伯益且戒其無荒；成王之賢，周公必戒其無逸。今陛下之德，將以為舜也，將以卓越成王也，臣敢不致其愛耶？惟願陛下益加懋德，正其本而不移；益廣求賢，操其幾而不失。防微杜漸，常若我祖宗創業之初；持盈守成，遠追古帝王致治之盛。久大之業，自是而可以無疆；熈皥之休，自是而可以不替。此則愚臣區區之誠，而亦陛下所欲聞之實也。陛下倘不以臣言為不可用，豈特愚臣之幸哉？臣干冒天威，不勝隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
On the matters addressed in Your Majesty’s imperial pronouncement, your servant has already briefly disclosed his sincere thoughts. Yet in my devoted heart there is something I cannot suppress. The achievements of government are difficult to preserve, and people readily become complacent. Thus, in one’s conduct one must constantly fear a lack of vigilance; even sagehood may falter through a moment’s inattention. Though Yu Shun was a sage, Bo Yi nevertheless admonished him against neglect; though King Cheng was worthy, the Duke of Zhou insisted on warning him against ease. Now Your Majesty’s virtue promises to equal Shun’s and far surpass King Cheng’s. Dare your servant fail to express his loving concern?
I ask only that Your Majesty strive still harder to cultivate virtue, setting the foundation aright and never departing from it; that you seek worthy men still more widely, grasping the critical workings of affairs without losing hold of them. Guard against the slightest signs of trouble and forestall their growth, remaining always as vigilant as our imperial ancestors at the founding of the dynasty. Preserve prosperity and safeguard what has been achieved, emulating the flourishing government of the ancient emperors and kings. From this, your enduring and great undertaking may know no bounds, and the blessings of radiant harmony may never decline. This is the humble sincerity of your foolish servant, and also the substance Your Majesty wishes to hear. If Your Majesty should judge your servant’s words usable, would the good fortune be that of your foolish servant alone? Your servant has presumed to affront Your Majesty’s heavenly might and is overwhelmed with fear and trembling. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
臣李廷相
臣對臣聞圖天下之大治者必急天下之大
務急天下之大務者必端天下之大本大務
者何任相是已大本者何脩身是已相不任
則事幾叢脞而不能以獨理身不脩則賢否
混淆而不能以周知是故為人君者不患天
下之難治而患不能任相不患輔相之非人
而患不能脩身身既脩矣而賢相之不得治
功之不成者未之有也欽惟
皇帝陛下英資天挺
===
===
聖德日新
臨御以來懐弘化理以圖天下之治者既無不
至網羅俊乂以弼天下之治者又無或遺然
猶
體道謙冲不自滿假進臣等于
廷降賜
清問俯詢治道首言三代守成之賢君末復究
以今日之時弊臣一介草茅何足以知之然
天下之事亦嘗展轉于胸中久矣有
君如此其忍負之用是掇拾所聞以對揚萬一在

臣對：臣聞圖天下之大治者，必急天下之大務；急天下之大務者，必端天下之大本。大務者何？任相是已。大本者何？脩身是已。相不任，則事幾叢脞而不能以獨理；身不脩，則賢否混淆而不能以周知。是故為人君者，不患天下之難治，而患不能任相；不患輔相之非人，而患不能脩身。身既脩矣，而賢相之不得、治功之不成者，未之有也。
欽惟皇帝陛下，英資天挺，聖德日新。臨御以來，懐弘化理，以圖天下之治者既無不至；網羅俊乂，以弼天下之治者又無或遺。然猶體道謙冲，不自滿假，進臣等于廷，降賜清問，俯詢治道，首言三代守成之賢君，末復究以今日之時弊。臣一介草茅，何足以知之？然天下之事，亦嘗展轉于胸中久矣。有君如此，其忍負之？用是掇拾所聞，以對揚萬一。在
translation_en:
Your servant, Li Tingxiang.
Your servant replies: I have heard that anyone who seeks great order throughout the realm must give priority to its most important affairs; anyone who gives priority to those affairs must first set right its fundamental foundation. What is the most important affair? Entrusting government to chief ministers. What is the fundamental foundation? Cultivating oneself. Unless chief ministers are entrusted with government, the affairs requiring attention become a tangled mass that the ruler cannot manage alone. Unless he cultivates himself, the worthy and unworthy become confused, and he cannot discern them all. Thus a ruler should worry not that the realm is difficult to govern, but that he cannot entrust government to chief ministers; not that his assisting ministers are unsuitable, but that he cannot cultivate himself. There has never been a ruler who, having cultivated himself, failed to obtain worthy chief ministers or to achieve good government.
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses outstanding gifts bestowed by Heaven, and that your sagely virtue is renewed daily. Since ascending the throne, you have cherished the aim of extending moral transformation and good government, leaving nothing undone in seeking order throughout the realm. You have gathered men of outstanding ability to assist in governing the realm, overlooking none. Yet you still embody the Way in humility, without complacency. You have brought us into your court and graciously bestowed your august questions, condescending to ask us about the way of government. You began by speaking of the worthy rulers of the Three Dynasties who preserved their inherited achievements, and concluded by probing the failings of our own times. Your servant is merely a man from the countryside: how could I know enough to answer? Nevertheless, the affairs of the realm have long occupied my thoughts. With such a ruler, how could I bear to fail him? I therefore gather what I have heard, hoping that my reply may acknowledge and give expression to even a fraction of your gracious intent. In…

昔三代之時創業之君如禹如湯如文武兢
兢業業至艱至危歷數十年而後大業始就
賢聖相承如啓如中宗高宗如成王康王世
守弗墜作史者以為美談論治者以為稱首

translation_en:
…in the ancient Three Dynasties, founding rulers such as Yu, Tang, and Kings Wen and Wu were ever vigilant and diligent. Through the greatest hardships and perils, they labored for decades before their great undertaking was accomplished. Worthy and sage rulers succeeded one another: Qi, Zhongzong, Gaozong, King Cheng, and King Kang preserved that undertaking generation after generation without letting it decline. Historians celebrated them, and those who discussed government ranked them foremost. There is certainly no room for dispute about this. I humbly reflect that our dynasty’s Emperor Taizu Gao swept away the non-Han Yuan and founded the realm; Emperor Taizong Wen then quelled internal strife and firmly secured the two capitals. Compared with Yu, Tang, and Kings Wen and Wu, their magnificent virtue and great achievements truly correspond, though belonging to different ages. To preserve and maintain this inheritance today, surpassing [?] the flourishing rule of Xia’s Qi, Zhongzong, Gaozong, King Cheng, and King Kang—is this not what your ignorant servant hopes for from Your Majesty? And is it not also why Your Majesty has put this policy question to your servant?
Yet Your Majesty’s purpose in questioning your servant concerns appointing chief ministers, whereas what your servant hopes for from Your Majesty is cultivation of your own person. In ancient times, at the court of the Yellow Emperor, six chief ministers were raised to office and Chiyou was executed; Heaven and Earth were brought into order, and divine spirits arrived. At the court of Shun of Yu, the Eight Primal Ones and Eight Talented Ones were appointed ministers, and the Four Wicked Ones were removed; wondrous creatures appeared, and phoenixes came in stately array. Yet commentators praise the Yellow Emperor not for his ability to appoint ministers but for his ability to cultivate virtue; they praise Shun not for his ability to appoint ministers but for his ability to hold fast to the Mean. Why is this? It is because success or failure in governing certainly depends upon the assisting ministers…

…while the worthiness or unworthiness of the chief ministers, in turn, has its root in the ruler himself. Confucius said: “Government depends upon men; one selects men through cultivating oneself.” Is this not what he meant? If even the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity could not govern apart from this principle, how could any ruler preserving an inherited realm abandon it and seek elsewhere? Your servant asks leave to speak of the worthy rulers of the Three Dynasties who preserved their inherited realms.
Qi reverently upheld the Way of Yu and applied himself energetically to action. He held a feast for the feudal lords at Diaotai, recalling the assembly at Tushan; he campaigned against the Youhu and addressed an oath to the six armies, approaching the example of the execution of Fangfeng. All songs of praise turned toward him, and all lawsuits were brought before him. Although this showed where Heaven’s mandate lay, the contribution of his reverent self-cultivation and sincere employment of Yi cannot be discounted.
Zhongzong and Gaozong of Shang turned calamities into auspicious signs and recovered Heaven’s mandate when it was about to fall away. They brought good order and peace to the Yin realm and reunited the people’s hearts after these had become estranged. The achievements of their restoration resounded conspicuously in people’s ears [?]. Examining how they accomplished this, we find that one was solemn, respectful, reverent, and fearful, measuring himself against Heaven’s mandate; those who protected and governed the royal house and reached the Lord on High included Yi Zhi and Wu Xian. The other pondered the Way in respectful silence, daring neither to neglect his duties nor to rest at ease; those with whom he had formerly studied outside the palace, and those whom he then established as chief ministers, included Gan Pan and Fu Yue. Such was these two rulers’ ability to cultivate themselves and appoint chief ministers. Can one say that the Shang house’s rule over the realm for more than six hundred years was not rooted in this?
Under Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou, the people embraced ritual propriety and righteousness, and all within the seas was at peace. Punishments were set aside unused, and the prisons stood empty. 周家八百餘年之天下謂不基於此耶由是
觀之則欲圖治者固不可不任相而欲任相
者又不可不脩身也故程頤曰聖王以求任

子與小人二儒之論可謂深知治體者矣治
天下者舎此獨何據哉今
聖明統治於上宰執輔治於下臣復何言然天下
之患每成於因循而人主之志常戒乎怠忽
故古之聖王非徒以禍患為可憂而尤以燕

translation_en:
…such as Duke Bi and Jun Chen. Such was the ability of these two rulers to cultivate themselves and appoint chief ministers. Could one say that the Zhou dynasty’s rule over the realm for more than eight hundred years was not founded upon this? Viewed in this light, anyone wishing to bring about good government must indeed appoint chief ministers, and anyone wishing to appoint chief ministers must also cultivate himself. Thus Cheng Yi said, “The sage kings gave priority to seeking and appointing assisting ministers.” Ouyang Xiu likewise said, “A ruler’s sagacity lies in distinguishing gentlemen from petty men.” These two scholars’ arguments may truly be said to show a profound understanding of the essentials of government. What else could those who govern the realm rely upon if they abandoned this?

Now Your sagacious Majesty governs above, while the chief ministers assist in government below. What more can your servant say? Yet the troubles of the realm often arise from complacently following established ways, and a sovereign must always guard his resolve against indolence and negligence. Thus the sage kings of antiquity regarded not only calamity as a cause for concern, but comfortable ease as especially to be feared. Security does not remain secure forever: the seeds of danger already lie hidden within it. Order does not remain orderly forever: the steps toward disorder are already gradually taking shape. Faults arise in the wake of abundance [?], and abuses emerge after prolonged peace. This is both a natural principle and an inevitable tendency.

Your servant observes that recent affairs of the state are indeed as described in Your Majesty’s policy question. At the risk of death, your servant ventures to speak of them to Your Majesty. Ritual and music are the means by which the realm is molded. When the great rites are established, their measured order accords with that of Heaven and Earth; when great music is performed, its harmony accords with that of Heaven and Earth. In the time of the imperial ancestors, ritual and music certainly flourished. Can they truly be said to do so now? Your servant sees that the custom of modest deference has already declined, while the tendency toward usurpation and seizure has yet to be extinguished, and sounds of peace and harmony…

絃誦之聲鮮聞雖有董學之官而櫌楚之威
亦廢況復如古之一道德同風俗者乎成周
===

自古矣我
祖宗因其法而行之未始不善邇年以來民偽日
滋晝一日壞斂於為私以相歎公然為黨以
相敝遂使勤勞王事者不一二而坐耗廩祿
者常千百選才之弊有不可言者矣虞舜有
三載考績三考黜陟幽明之法是課績亦肇

祖宗因其法而行之未始不善比年以來柔名不

音寡倡，而淫哇之習方興。宗伯鴻臚之所陳，祗循諸故事；太常教坊之所奏，徒尚夫新聲。况復如古之安上下、和神人者乎？教化所以維持天下者也，置天下於道德仁義，洽德澤於鳥獸草木。祖宗之時，教化固已行矣，今果能如此否乎？臣見夫饕餮之行日生，而廉耻之維日壞；奔競之門方啓，而禮義之澤寢微。雖有掌教之職，而絃誦之聲鮮聞；雖有董學之官，而榎楚之威亦廢。况復如古之一道德、同風俗者乎？

成周有鄉舉里選、三年一大比之法，是選才已肇自古矣。我祖宗因其法而行之，未始不善。邇年以來，民偽日滋，畫一日壞，敢於為私以相欺，公然為黨以相蔽，遂使勤勞王事者不一二，而坐耗廩禄者常千百。選才之弊，有不可言者矣。

虞舜有三載考績、三考黜陟幽明之法，是課績亦肇自古矣。我□宗因其法而行之，未始不善。比年以來，采名不□□，誅文不誅意，是非徒取於風聞，黜陟祗
translation_en:
…harmonious music finds few advocates, while the vogue for licentious sounds is just arising. What the Minister of Rites and the Court of State Ceremonial set forth merely follows established precedents; what the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the Music Office perform prizes only novel sounds. How, then, could these bring peace to those above and below and harmony between spirits and men, as in antiquity? Moral instruction is what sustains the realm: it establishes all under Heaven in the Way, virtue, benevolence, and righteousness, and extends beneficent influence even to birds, beasts, plants, and trees. In the time of our imperial ancestors, moral instruction was indeed put into practice. Can it truly be so today? Your servant sees greedy conduct increasing daily and the bonds of integrity and shame deteriorating daily; avenues for competitive advancement are opening, while the beneficent influence of ritual propriety and righteousness gradually diminishes. Although there are posts responsible for instruction, the sounds of strings and recitation are seldom heard; although there are officials supervising education, even the disciplinary authority of the rod has fallen into disuse. How, then, could these unify moral principles and bring uniformity to customs, as in antiquity?

The Zhou dynasty had a system of recommending men through townships and selecting them through villages, with a great assessment every three years. Thus, the selection of talent originated in antiquity. Our imperial ancestors adopted and implemented this system, and it was sound from the outset. In recent years, however, deceit among the people has increased daily, and uniform standards have deteriorated daily. Men dare to pursue private interests and deceive one another; they openly form factions and shield one another. Consequently, scarcely one or two labor diligently in royal service, while hundreds and thousands habitually sit idle, consuming official stipends. The abuses in the selection of talent are beyond telling.

Shun of Yu had a system of evaluating performance every three years and, after three evaluations, dismissing the incompetent and promoting the able. Thus, performance evaluation likewise originated in antiquity. Our imperial ancestors [?] adopted and implemented this system, and it was sound from the outset. In recent years, however, reputation has been accepted without… [?]; the wording is condemned, rather than the intention. Judgments of right and wrong are drawn solely from hearsay, and dismissals and promotions merely…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
憑其毀譽遂使賢勞者被黜而闒茸者獲陞
課績之弊有不可既者矣至於征賦之法所
以足國用而給百官也
國初賦不加倍而用度自充况蠲租之詔屢頒
甚或全賜天下
今非其時矣而反不逮焉何哉臣竊聞之勸農
之榜委於墻壁催租之吏害及雞豚財已竭
而斂不休民既窮而賦愈急殆有不勝其可
痛者兵刑之令所以禁姦宄而遏暴亂也
國初治方粗創而人心自齊况勝國之習未除
===
甚或專用兵刑
今非其時矣而反不及焉何哉臣又聞之行伍
之卒甘於逃亡比擬之文恣為輕重將恃閥
閱以為高吏弄新巧以為威殆有不勝其可
慨者是則禮樂也教化也選才也課績也征
賦也兵刑也皆我
祖宗究歷代之制參百王之宜而啓億萬年無疆
之休者也
聖子神孫重熙累洽之時惟在持循保守之而已
耳今其弊乃如此是果奉行之者不肯為

憑其毀譽，遂使賢勞者被黜，而闒茸者獲陞，課績之弊有不可既者矣。至於征賦之法，所以足國用而給百官也。國初賦不加倍，而用度自充，况蠲租之詔屢頒，甚或全賜天下。今非其時矣，而反不逮焉，何哉？臣竊聞之：勸農之榜委於墻壁，催租之吏害及雞豚，財已竭而斂不休，民既窮而賦愈急，殆有不勝其可痛者。兵刑之令，所以禁姦宄而遏暴亂也。國初治方粗創，而人心自齊，况勝國之習未除，甚或專用兵刑。今非其時矣，而反不及焉，何哉？臣又聞之：行伍之卒甘於逃亡，比擬之文恣為輕重，將恃閥閱以為高，吏弄新巧以為威，殆有不勝其可慨者。

是則禮樂也，教化也，選才也，課績也，征賦也，兵刑也，皆我祖宗究歷代之制、參百王之宜，而啓億萬年無疆之休者也。聖子神孫重熙累洽之時，惟在持循保守之而已耳。今其弊乃如此，是果奉行之者不肯為
translation_en:
…rely on the disparagement or praise they receive. Thus worthy and hardworking men are dismissed, while the base and incompetent gain promotion. The abuses in evaluating service are inexhaustible. As for the system of taxation, its purpose is to provide sufficient funds for the state and support the officials. At the dynasty’s founding, taxes were not doubled, yet funds naturally sufficed for expenditure. Moreover, edicts remitting taxes were repeatedly issued, sometimes even granting complete remission throughout the realm. Those circumstances no longer prevail today, yet results fall short of what was achieved then. Why is this? Your servant has heard that proclamations encouraging agriculture are left neglected on walls, while the depredations of tax collectors extend even to chickens and pigs. Resources are exhausted, yet exactions never cease; the people are already impoverished, yet demands for taxes grow more urgent. The distress this occasions is almost unbearable.

Military and penal ordinances serve to restrain wrongdoing and suppress violence and disorder. At the dynasty’s founding, government had only just been established, yet the people’s hearts were naturally united. Furthermore, the habits of the preceding dynasty had not yet been eliminated, and sometimes military force and punishment alone were employed. Those circumstances no longer prevail today, yet results fall short of what was achieved then. Why is this? Your servant has also heard that soldiers in the ranks readily desert, and that provisions applying the law by analogy are arbitrarily made lenient or severe. Generals rely on their pedigrees and records of merit to exalt themselves, while functionaries manipulate novel devices to display their power. The cause for lamentation is almost unbearable.

Thus ritual and music, moral instruction, the selection of talent, the evaluation of service, taxation, and military and penal affairs are all means by which our dynastic ancestors examined the institutions of successive dynasties, weighed what was appropriate in the practices of the many former kings, and inaugurated boundless blessings for countless ages. In an age when their sage sons and divine grandsons inherit successive generations of prosperity and good government, all that is required is to uphold, follow, preserve, and maintain these institutions. Yet their abuses have now come to this. Is it truly that those charged with implementing them are unwilling to act for…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下盡心耶抑
陛下所以任用之者有未至耶臣愚以為回天下
之勢者在機而不在力運天下之機者在上
而不在下
陛下誠能脩身以為任相之本任相以為輔治之
資則
祖宗之時何患其不可復而前代之隆何患其不
可及哉且今
陛下於平居之日朝夕而親信之者何人賜譴而
震怒之者何人定計决策誠以任用之者何
===
人越次躐等召而訊問之者何人臣皆未之
聞焉此臣惓惓之忠所以必欲
陛下勤於任相也然輔相之賢否君子小人之情
狀誠未易知苟無道以照之安知其不以賢
為不肖以不肖為賢以君子為小人以小人
為君子乎故臣以脩身之說為
陛下獻焉夫身固任相之本而心又一身之本故
堯舜之授受必曰人心道心而湯武之作聖
必曰宅心制心良以心既正則身無不脩而
輔相之賢亦無不得矣伏願

punctuated:
陛下盡心耶？抑陛下所以任用之者有未至耶？臣愚以為，回天下之勢者在機而不在力，運天下之機者在上而不在下。陛下誠能脩身以為任相之本，任相以為輔治之資，則祖宗之時何患其不可復，而前代之隆何患其不可及哉？且今陛下於平居之日，朝夕而親信之者何人？賜譴而震怒之者何人？定計决策，誠以任用之者何人？越次躐等，召而訊問之者何人？臣皆未之聞焉。此臣惓惓之忠所以必欲陛下勤於任相也。
然輔相之賢否、君子小人之情狀，誠未易知。苟無道以照之，安知其不以賢為不肖，以不肖為賢，以君子為小人，以小人為君子乎？故臣以脩身之說為陛下獻焉。夫身固任相之本，而心又一身之本。故堯舜之授受必曰人心、道心，而湯武之作聖必曰宅心、制心，良以心既正，則身無不脩，而輔相之賢亦無不得矣。伏願
translation_en:
…devote themselves wholeheartedly to Your Majesty? Or is there some shortcoming in how Your Majesty employs them? In my humble judgment, reversing the course of the realm depends on the crucial pivot, not on force; setting that pivot in motion rests with those above, not those below. If Your Majesty can truly cultivate yourself as the foundation for appointing chief ministers, and appoint chief ministers as a means of assisting your rule, why fear that the age of your imperial ancestors cannot be restored, or that the flourishing achievements of former dynasties cannot be equaled? Moreover, in Your Majesty’s daily life today, whom do you keep close and trust morning and evening? Whom do you reprimand in thunderous anger? Whom do you truly employ to formulate plans and decide policies? Whom do you summon for questioning, passing over the customary order and distinctions of rank? I have heard of none. It is because of my earnest loyalty that I am so intent on urging Your Majesty to attend diligently to appointing chief ministers.
Yet the worthiness or unworthiness of chief ministers, and the true dispositions of exemplary and petty men, are indeed difficult to discern. Without a way to illuminate them, how can you be sure that you will not mistake the worthy for the unworthy, the unworthy for the worthy, exemplary men for petty men, and petty men for exemplary men? It is therefore that I present to Your Majesty this argument for self-cultivation. One’s own person is indeed the foundation for appointing chief ministers, while the mind is in turn the foundation of one’s entire person. Thus, in the transmission of rule from Yao to Shun, they invariably spoke of the human mind and the mind of the Way; and in attaining sagehood, Tang and Wu invariably spoke of establishing the mind and regulating the mind. This is truly because, once the mind is rectified, the person cannot fail to be cultivated, and worthy chief ministers cannot fail to be obtained. I humbly wish that…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
陛下察理欲危微之幾而敬畏之是崇懋精一執
中之學而帝王之是憲盤樂怠傲此心之鴆
毒也
陛下必居之以勤竒技淫巧此心之蟊賊也
陛下必守之以儉忠鯁之言
陛下勿以逆意而罪之欲其擴此心也諂諛之說
陛下勿以遜志而從之恐其移此心也至于
禁密之地若可少怠矣必惕然而思曰吾心得
無有失乎得無異於坐朝之時乎細微之事
若可少肆矣必惕然而恐曰吾心得無有失
===
乎得無間於臨政之際乎夫然則
聖心洞然中外融徹而身烏有不脩者哉由是而
任相則某也為賢某也為否某也為君子某
也為小人舉錯一出於至公是非不謬於偏
聽一相得而百職自舉百職舉而萬化自行
將見禮樂惟其人而天下以陶以鎔兵刑惟
其人而天下以威以肅語教化則脩明語征
賦則充實司薦舉者不敢以桃李為私恩而
所選皆真才矣典銓衡者不敢以催科為上
最而所課皆實績矣由是言之則圖治必本

punctuated: 陛下察理欲危微之幾，而敬畏之是崇；懋精一執中之學，而帝王之是憲。盤樂怠傲，此心之鴆毒也，陛下必居之以勤；竒技淫巧，此心之蟊賊也，陛下必守之以儉。忠鯁之言，陛下勿以逆意而罪之，欲其擴此心也；諂諛之說，陛下勿以遜志而從之，恐其移此心也。至于禁密之地，若可少怠矣，必惕然而思曰：「吾心得無有失乎？得無異於坐朝之時乎？」細微之事，若可少肆矣，必惕然而恐曰：「吾心得無有失乎？得無間於臨政之際乎？」夫然則聖心洞然，中外融徹，而身烏有不脩者哉？由是而任相，則某也為賢，某也為否，某也為君子，某也為小人，舉錯一出於至公，是非不謬於偏聽。一相得而百職自舉，百職舉而萬化自行。將見禮樂惟其人，而天下以陶以鎔；兵刑惟其人，而天下以威以肅。語教化則脩明，語征賦則充實。司薦舉者不敢以桃李為私恩，而所選皆真才矣；典銓衡者不敢以催科為上最，而所課皆實績矣。由是言之，則圖治必本
translation_en:
…Your Majesty discern the subtle beginnings of moral principle and selfish desire—the precariousness of the human mind and the subtlety of the moral mind—and exalt reverence and awe; diligently pursue the learning of refinement, single-mindedness, and holding fast to the Mean, and take the ancient emperors and kings as your models. Indulgence in pleasure, indolence, and arrogance are deadly poison to this mind: Your Majesty must sustain it through diligence. Exotic devices and extravagant craftsmanship are pests that prey upon this mind: Your Majesty must guard it through frugality. Do not punish loyal and forthright words because they offend your wishes, for their purpose is to broaden this mind. Do not heed flattering words because they accord with your inclinations, for they may sway this mind. When in the secluded inner palace, where a little relaxation might seem permissible, you must think with vigilance: “Might my mind have gone astray? Might it differ from how it is when I sit at court?” In minor matters, where a little license might seem permissible, you must ask yourself with vigilance and apprehension: “Might my mind have gone astray? Might it diverge from how it is when I attend to government?” Then your sagely mind will be perfectly clear, inwardly and outwardly transparent throughout. How could your person remain uncultivated?

If you appoint a chief minister on this basis, you will recognize who is worthy and who is not, who is a gentleman and who is a petty man. Appointments and dismissals will proceed entirely from the utmost impartiality, and judgments of right and wrong will not be distorted by listening to only one side. Once the right chief minister is found, the duties of all offices will naturally be fulfilled; once those duties are fulfilled, the myriad transformations will naturally proceed. You will then see ritual and music entrusted to the right men, through whom all under Heaven will be molded and refined; military affairs and punishments entrusted to the right men, through whom all under Heaven will be awed and disciplined. Moral instruction will be cultivated and made clear; tax revenues will be abundant. Those responsible for recommending men will not dare treat their protégés as recipients of personal favors, and all whom they select will possess genuine talent. Those responsible for personnel selection and evaluation will not dare rate the collection of taxes as the highest achievement, and all that they assess will be substantive accomplishments. Viewed in this light, the pursuit of good government must be rooted…

title: 弘治十五年進士登科錄
text:
於任相而任相必本於脩身也明矣
陛下誠能採而用之則
陛下之心即
祖宗之心全體妙用質之前聞而無忝
陛下之治即
祖宗之治豐功偉烈建諸天地而不悖
皇圖自此而益隆世道于焉而復古夏商周之
賢君固不得專美於昔而重華丕承之盛將
復見於
今矣臣學不足以博古知不足以通今一得之

而必見之行勿以為常談而必施之治則愚
臣幸甚天下幸甚臣干冒
宸嚴不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對

賢君固不得專美於昔而重華二帝之盛將
復見於
今矣臣學不足以博古知不足以通今一得之
===
愚上塵
天聽詞雖涉於粗鄙情實發於忠誠儻
陛下寬其斧鉞之誅畧其狂妄之罪勿以為迂遠
而必見之行勿以為常談而必施之治則愚
臣幸甚天下幸甚臣干冒
宸嚴不勝戰慄隕越之至臣謹對
punctuated:
於任相，而任相必本於脩身也，明矣。陛下誠能採而用之，則陛下之心即祖宗之心，全體妙用，質之前聞而無忝；陛下之治即祖宗之治，豐功偉烈，建諸天地而不悖。皇圖自此而益隆，世道于焉而復古。夏商周之賢君固不得專美於昔，而重華丕承之盛將復見於今矣。
臣學不足以博古，知不足以通今，一得之愚，上塵天聽。詞雖涉於粗鄙，情實發於忠誠。儻陛下寬其斧鉞之誅，畧其狂妄之罪，勿以為迂逺而必見之行，勿以為常談而必施之治，則愚臣幸甚，天下幸甚。臣干冒宸嚴，不勝戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…upon appointing a chief minister, and that appointing a chief minister must in turn be rooted in cultivating oneself: this is clear. If Your Majesty can truly adopt and employ these proposals, then Your Majesty’s heart will be the very heart of your imperial ancestors, complete in its substance and wondrous in its functioning, bearing comparison with the records of the past without disgrace. Your Majesty’s governance will be the very governance of your imperial ancestors, its abundant achievements and mighty deeds established between Heaven and Earth without contravening their order. The imperial enterprise will thereby flourish still further, and the ways of the world will return to those of antiquity. The worthy rulers of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou will assuredly no longer monopolize the glory of the past; the splendid succession of Chonghua, the sage Shun, who grandly carried on his predecessor’s achievements, will be seen again today.
Your servant’s learning is insufficient for a broad understanding of antiquity, and his knowledge insufficient for comprehending the present. With this single foolish insight, I presume to trouble Your Majesty’s hearing. Though my words verge on the crude and vulgar, my feelings truly spring from loyalty and sincerity. If Your Majesty will spare me execution by the axe and overlook the offense of my reckless presumption, neither dismissing these proposals as impractical and far-fetched but assuredly putting them into action, nor treating them as commonplace talk but assuredly applying them in governance, then your foolish servant will be most fortunate, and all under Heaven most fortunate. Your servant has presumed to offend your imperial majesty and is overcome with trembling and dread of utter ruin. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
